title: Extracellular Recording: Spikes to Brain Waves
summary: Learn how electrodes outside neurons capture spikes from single cells, populations and rhythmic oscillations in behaving animals.

lessons.title: Single-Unit Recording: Hubel, Wiesel and the Metal Microelectrode

levels.kid:
Your brain cells talk using tiny electric blips called **spikes**. Scientists wanted to hear just one cell talking.

So they made a needle much thinner than a hair, out of a strong metal called **tungsten**. They slid it gently into the brain until its tip sat right next to one cell, not inside it.

Each time the cell fired, the needle picked up a tiny blip. A speaker turned each blip into a click, like popcorn popping!

Two scientists, **David Hubel** and **Torsten Wiesel**, listened to cells in the part of the brain that handles seeing. Some cells clicked fast only when a line at a certain tilt appeared. Seeing starts with simple lines! Their discovery won a Nobel Prize.
levels.hs:
**Single-unit recording** means measuring the electrical activity of one neuron at a time. Neurons signal with **action potentials** (spikes), brief pulses lasting about 1 millisecond. In **extracellular** recording, a fine electrode sits in the fluid just outside the cell membrane, not inside the cell. When the neuron fires, current crossing its membrane creates a tiny voltage change nearby, only about 50 to 500 **microvolts** (millionths of a volt), so it must be amplified. Played through a speaker, each spike sounds like a click.

In 1957 **David Hubel** made a tough electrode by electrolytically sharpening a **tungsten** wire and coating it with insulation except at the very tip. It could be pushed through brain tissue for hours without bending.

A real example: Hubel and **Torsten Wiesel** recorded from the cat's **primary visual cortex (V1)**. Small round spots of light, which drive retinal cells well, did little. Then one cell fired furiously as the edge of a glass slide moved past in their projector. Most V1 neurons, they discovered, respond best to edges or bars at a particular tilt, called **orientation selectivity**. The region of space where a stimulus changes a cell's firing is its **receptive field**.

They later showed that closing one eye in young kittens rewired V1. In 1981 they shared the Nobel Prize with Roger Sperry.
levels.college:
**Why extracellular?** An intracellular electrode sees the full ~100 mV action potential but injures cells and rarely survives brain movement. An extracellular tip only needs to sit near a neuron, so recordings last hours, even in awake animals.

**The physics.** During a spike, current flows into the cell near the soma and axon initial segment and returns outward through the dendrites. Near the soma the electrode sees a sharp negative deflection followed by a smaller positive phase, all within about 1 ms. Amplitude falls steeply with distance, so a unit is usually isolated only within roughly 50 µm of the tip.

**Electrode and signal chain.**
- Metal microelectrodes (tungsten, platinum-iridium, stainless steel) with tips a few micrometres across and impedances of roughly 0.5 to 10 MΩ at 1 kHz. A fine, high-impedance tip listens to a small volume near one cell, aiding isolation.
- A headstage and differential amplifier compare the tip with a reference electrode.
- A band-pass filter of about 300 to 5,000 Hz keeps spikes; slower signals form the local field potential.
- Spikes are detected by threshold crossing and monitored on an oscilloscope and loudspeaker.

**Is it one neuron?** A good single unit has a consistent waveform and almost no inter-spike intervals shorter than about 2 ms, because the refractory period forbids them. Mixed signals from several cells are **multi-unit activity**.

**Analysis.** Rasters show spikes on each trial; a **peri-stimulus time histogram (PSTH)** averages firing rate over time; a **tuning curve** plots rate against a feature such as orientation.

**Hubel and Wiesel's findings** (anesthetized cats, later monkeys):
- **Simple cells** have separate ON and OFF subregions; **complex cells** respond to an oriented bar anywhere within a larger region.
- **Columns**: neighbouring cells share orientation and eye preference (ocular dominance).
- **Monocular deprivation** during an early critical period left most cells driven by the open eye.

Edward Evarts later recorded motor cortex units in awake, trained monkeys, launching behaving-animal electrophysiology.
levels.phd:
**Biophysics.** Brain tissue behaves approximately as an ohmic volume conductor, so the extracellular potential is a distance-weighted sum of transmembrane currents (ionic plus capacitive). The spike waveform reflects membrane current, not membrane voltage, and near the soma roughly resembles the inverted first derivative of the intracellular action potential. Henze et al. (2000), recording CA1 pyramidal cells intracellularly and extracellularly at once, found that units were reliably separable within about 50 µm and detectable to about 140 µm, a volume holding around a thousand neurons. Most are never seen.

**Sampling bias.** High-impedance electrodes favor large somata with strong dipoles (layer 5 pyramidal cells, Betz cells) and neurons that respond to the search stimulus. Shoham, O'Connor and Segev (2006) argued that many cortical neurons are nearly silent, a "dark matter" classic studies missed. Firing rates are heavy-tailed, roughly lognormal (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014).

**Identifying cell types.** Waveform width separates narrow-spiking (putative fast-spiking parvalbumin interneurons) from broad-spiking (putative pyramidal) units, imperfectly. Projection neurons are identified by **antidromic activation**: stimulating the axon target evokes a fixed-latency spike, confirmed by the **collision test**, in which the evoked spike vanishes when stimulation follows a spontaneous spike within the conduction time. Juxtacellular labeling (Pinault, 1996) fills the recorded cell with neurobiotin.

**Pharmacology at the unit.** Multibarrel micropipettes paired recording with **microiontophoresis**; Curtis, Phillis and Watkins (1959-60) used this to show glutamate excites central neurons, founding excitatory amino acid research.

**Lineage and debates.** Adrian's single-fiber work (1920s) established rate coding; Kuffler (1953), Hubel and Wiesel's mentor, described center-surround retinal receptive fields; Mountcastle (1957) found somatosensory columns. Hubel and Wiesel's 1959 and 1962 *Journal of Physiology* papers proposed that simple cells arise from aligned LGN inputs and complex cells from pooled simple cells. Feedforward alignment gained support (Reid and Alonso, 1995; Ferster et al., 1996), but recurrent cortical circuits shape tuning, and simple versus complex is better viewed as a continuum: simple cells give a modulation ratio F1/F0 > 1 to drifting gratings (Skottun et al., 1991).
levels.expert:
**Rig craft.** Most failed sessions are noise problems: 50/60 Hz mains pickup, ground loops, and movement artifact in behaving animals. Practitioners use single-point grounding, keep the headstage close to the electrode, and listen: a well-isolated unit gives a crisp click standing above the background hash. Advance slowly with a hydraulic or stepper microdrive, because cortex dimples and then rebounds, sweeping cells past the tip; letting tissue settle improves stability.

**Confounds.** Anesthetics change what you measure. Urethane, isoflurane and barbiturates alter cortical state, spontaneous rates and some tuning properties, so awake head-fixed or freely moving preparations are now standard where behavior matters. Chronic implants trigger a foreign-body response (microglial activation, astrocytic scarring, local neuron loss) that typically erodes unit yield over weeks to months. Carbon-fiber electrodes under ~10 µm and low-impedance coatings such as PEDOT or platinum black aim to cut damage while preserving signal-to-noise.

**Pharmacology classics.** Bunney, Aghajanian and Roth (1973) identified midbrain dopamine neurons by their slow, broad, often bursting spikes. Dopamine agonists such as apomorphine slowed their firing, whereas D2-antagonist antipsychotics such as haloperidol increased it, revealing inhibitory somatodendritic **D2 autoreceptors**. Grace and Bunney (1984) separated tonic single-spike from phasic burst firing, a distinction central to Schultz's reward-prediction-error recordings.

**The operating room.** The same metal-microelectrode logic guides deep brain stimulation surgery. During **microelectrode recording (MER)**, the team hears background activity change as the tip crosses structures; in Parkinson's disease the subthalamic nucleus shows dense, irregular, fast firing, often with tremor-locked or beta-rhythmic cells, helping confirm target borders before the permanent lead goes in. Whether MER improves outcomes over image-guided targeting alone is still debated.

**Open questions.** How representative are the loud, easily isolated neurons that built textbook neuroscience? Tagging methods help, but single-electrode datasets remain biased toward large, active cells. Hubel and Wiesel's hierarchy also shaped computing: Fukushima's neocognitron (1980) and later convolutional neural networks borrowed simple-like and complex-like processing stages.

keyPoints: Extracellular electrodes sit just outside a neuron and detect spikes of about 50-500 microvolts
Hubel's 1957 electrolytically sharpened tungsten microelectrode made long, stable recordings possible
Units are isolated within about 50 µm; a refractory gap in inter-spike intervals marks a single neuron
Spike band is filtered around 300-5,000 Hz; rasters, PSTHs and tuning curves summarize firing
Hubel and Wiesel found orientation-selective simple and complex cells and cortical columns in V1
Monocular deprivation revealed a critical period; Nobel Prize 1981 shared with Roger Sperry

test.q: In extracellular single-unit recording, where does the electrode tip sit?

About one to five volts

About one nanovolt or less

Small round spots of light
Edges at a particular tilt

test.q: In Hubel and Wiesel's famous early discovery, a cat cortical cell fired strongly when:

test.q: Why is a fine, high-impedance tip useful for isolating a single neuron?
choices: It stimulates neurons to fire more often
It boosts the voltage each neuron produces
It removes the need for any amplifier
It listens to a small volume near one cell

test.q: A band-pass filter for recording spikes typically passes about:
choices: 1 to 50 Hz
0.1 to 100 Hz
10 to 60 Hz
test.explain: Spikes last about 1 ms, so their energy is in the hundreds to thousands of hertz. Lower frequencies make up the local field potential.

test.q: Which feature suggests recorded spikes come from one neuron rather than several?
choices: Spikes of many different shapes and sizes
A large hum at 50 or 60 Hz
Firing that rises with stimulus contrast
Almost no intervals shorter than about 2 ms
test.explain: A single neuron's refractory period prevents very short inter-spike intervals. Varied waveforms suggest multiple cells; a 50/60 Hz hum is mains noise.

test.q: Kittens with one eye closed during an early critical period showed:
choices: No change in cortical responses
Equal responses from both eyes
Cells driven mostly by the open eye
Faster responses from the closed eye
test.explain: Monocular deprivation shifted ocular dominance so most V1 cells responded mainly to the open eye.

Edgar Adrian
Stephen Kuffler
Roger Sperry
test.explain: Roger Sperry shared the 1981 prize. Adrian won in 1932, and Kuffler was Hubel and Wiesel's mentor.

test.q: Which metal did David Hubel electrolytically sharpen to make his 1957 microelectrode?
test.explain: Tungsten is stiff and strong, so a sharpened, insulated tungsten wire could be pushed through brain tissue for hours.

test.explain: Mapping receptive fields with spots and bars was the core of Hubel and Wiesel's method.

advancedTest.q: Because extracellular spike amplitude falls steeply with distance, a high-impedance electrode in cortex will tend to:
choices: Over-sample large, active cells and miss silent ones
Detect single neurons up to several millimetres away
Sample neuron types in proportion to their abundance
Favor small interneurons with weak membrane currents
advancedTest.explain: Large somata with strong dipoles and responsive cells produce the biggest nearby signals, so they dominate; nearly silent neurons form unseen 'dark matter.'

advancedTest.q: A V1 unit shows a strongly modulated response at a drifting grating's temporal frequency, with F1/F0 > 1. It is best classified as:
choices: A simple cell
An LGN relay neuron
A complex cell
A retinal ganglion cell
advancedTest.explain: A modulation ratio above 1 is the standard criterion for simple cells. Complex cells respond with an elevated unmodulated rate, and the unit is in V1, not the LGN or retina.

advancedTest.q: Stimulating a target region evokes a fixed-latency spike in your recorded unit. Which result best confirms the spike is antidromic?
choices: The evoked spike latency jitters widely across trials
The evoked spike persists when stimuli follow spontaneous spikes
The evoked spike grows larger with stronger stimulation
The evoked spike vanishes when timed just after a spontaneous one
advancedTest.explain: In the collision test, a spontaneous orthodromic spike travelling down the axon cancels the antidromic one if stimulation falls within the conduction time. Persistence would argue against a direct axonal projection.

advancedTest.q: Apomorphine slows recorded midbrain dopamine neuron firing, while haloperidol increases it. The best interpretation is:
choices: Antagonists block potassium channels in the cells
D1 receptors on the cells excite their firing
D2 autoreceptors on the cells inhibit their firing
Agonists act as local anaesthetics on the cells
advancedTest.explain: Bunney, Aghajanian and Roth's results fit inhibitory somatodendritic D2 autoreceptors: activating them slows firing, and blocking them removes the brake. Excitatory D1 receptors would predict the opposite effect of the agonist.

lessons.title: Tetrodes and Spike Sorting

levels.kid:
Imagine a busy party where lots of people are talking. If you hold up one microphone, all the voices get mixed together. But if you put four microphones in a little bunch, each voice sounds a bit louder in the microphone closest to that person. By comparing the four, you can tell who said what!

Brain cells, called **neurons**, talk with tiny electric beeps called **spikes**. Scientists slide a **tetrode** into the brain. A tetrode is four wires twisted together, thinner than a hair.

Each neuron's beep looks a little different on the four wires. A computer groups the beeps that match. This is called **spike sorting**. Now scientists know which cell beeped, and exactly when!
levels.hs:
Neurons communicate with brief electrical pulses called **action potentials**, or **spikes**. Each one lasts about a millisecond. An electrode placed just outside neurons, in the fluid between cells, can pick up these spikes. This is called **extracellular recording**. The catch is that one wire tip hears several nearby neurons at once, and spikes from two cells the same distance away can look almost identical.

The **tetrode** solves this. It is four insulated wires, each about 12 micrometers thick (several times thinner than a human hair), twisted into one bundle so their tips sit only tens of micrometers apart. A neuron close to wire 1 produces a big spike on wire 1 and smaller ones on wires 2, 3 and 4. A different neuron makes a different pattern. You use two ears to locate a sound in the same way that four wires let scientists tell cells apart.

**Spike sorting** is the process of assigning each recorded spike to the neuron that fired it:
- Detect spikes that cross a voltage threshold
- Measure features, such as the spike's height on each wire
- Group similar spikes into **clusters**, each ideally one neuron, called a **single unit**

A real example: in 2005, Edvard and May-Britt Moser's lab used tetrodes in rats to discover **grid cells**, neurons that fire in a hexagonal pattern as an animal explores. That work shared the 2014 Nobel Prize with John O'Keefe, who discovered place cells.
levels.college:
Extracellular spikes are tiny, from tens to a few hundred microvolts, and their amplitude falls steeply with distance from the cell body. That distance dependence is the key to the tetrode.

**History.** McNaughton, O'Keefe and Barnes introduced the two-wire **stereotrode** in 1983. Recce and O'Keefe extended the idea to four wires. Wilson and McNaughton's 1993 study used multiple tetrodes to record dozens of rat hippocampal place cells at the same time, and showed that the ensemble's activity could decode the animal's position.

**Hardware.** Tetrodes are usually twisted nichrome or platinum-iridium wire (roughly 12-18 µm). Tips are **gold-plated** to lower impedance, commonly to around 150-300 kΩ at 1 kHz, which reduces thermal noise. Many tetrodes are loaded into a **microdrive** or "hyperdrive" so each one can be lowered independently over days toward a target layer, such as the CA1 pyramidal layer.

**The sorting pipeline.**
- **Filter** the raw signal to roughly 300 Hz-6 kHz (0.3-6 kHz) to separate spikes from slower field potentials.
- **Detect** events crossing a threshold, often 4-5 times a noise estimate. A robust estimate uses the median absolute signal divided by 0.6745, because spikes would inflate a standard deviation.
- **Align** waveforms on their peaks and extract **features**: peak amplitude on each of the four channels, energy, or **principal components** that compress each waveform into a few informative numbers.
- **Cluster** points in feature space. This can be done by hand (**cluster cutting**: drawing boundaries in programs like MClust) or automatically (KlustaKwik, a Gaussian mixture method).
- **Check quality.** A true single unit should show almost no inter-spike intervals shorter than about 1-2 ms (the **refractory period**). Clusters that fail are labeled **multi-unit activity**. Metrics such as **isolation distance** and **L-ratio** measure how well a cluster is separated from its neighbors.

**Cell types.** In hippocampus and cortex, units with narrow waveforms and high firing rates are classed as putative **fast-spiking interneurons**. Broader, low-rate, bursting units are putative pyramidal cells. The word "putative" matters: waveform shape is an inference, not proof.
levels.phd:
**Biophysics.** In a volume conductor, a point current source produces V = I/(4πσr). A soma with return currents in its dendrites behaves more like a dipole, though, so extracellular spike amplitude decays faster than 1/r. Simultaneous intracellular-extracellular recordings in CA1 (Henze et al., 2000) showed that spikes are well above noise only within about 50 µm of a soma, and detectable out to roughly 140 µm. Buzsáki estimated that about a thousand neurons lie within that 140 µm radius, yet a good tetrode yields perhaps 5-20 well-isolated units. The rest are silent, fire too sparsely to form clusters, or are buried in background "hash."

**Ground truth.** Harris et al. (2000) recorded one CA1 cell intracellularly while a tetrode sat nearby, which provided known spike times. Errors split into **false positives** (other cells' spikes included) and **false negatives** (true spikes missed). Tetrodes outperformed single wires. An optimal ellipsoidal boundary in feature space beat human operators, whose errors were substantial and variable. This work motivated KlustaKwik, a classification expectation-maximization fit of Gaussian mixtures that chooses the number of clusters automatically.

**Why clusters misbehave.**
- **Bursting**: CA1 complex-spike bursts show progressive amplitude decrement at intervals of a few ms, so one cell can smear into an elongated cluster or be split into two. Amplitude ratios across channels stay roughly constant, which is a useful diagnostic.
- **Noise** is non-Gaussian and correlated across channels, because much of it is the spikes of distant neurons.
- **Overlaps**: when two neurons fire within about 1 ms, their waveforms sum into hybrids that fit neither template. Combined with detector dead time, this produces artifactual dips near zero lag in cross-correlograms between units on the same tetrode.
- **Drift**: slow electrode movement changes amplitudes over hours.

**Algorithms.** Alternatives to Gaussian mixtures include:
- Wave_clus (Quiroga, Nadasdy & Ben-Shaul, 2004), which uses wavelet features and superparamagnetic clustering
- Template matching, which can resolve overlaps by subtracting fitted templates
- MountainSort (Chung et al., 2017), built on the density-based ISO-SPLIT method

**Payoff.** Ensemble recordings revealed hippocampal **replay**. Wilson and McNaughton (1994) showed that place-cell pairs active together during running were preferentially co-active during later sleep. This finding is a foundation of research on systems memory consolidation.
levels.expert:
**Sorting is a modeling choice that shapes results.** Sorting errors are not random. False negatives concentrate during bursts and near-synchronous firing, so they bias estimates of synchrony, burst propensity and spike-timing correlations, which are the very quantities ensemble studies care about. Over-splitting inflates neuron counts and can fabricate "functional cell types," while over-merging blurs tuning. Report quality metrics for each unit rather than a single inclusion label. Common cutoffs (isolation distance >20, L-ratio <0.05; Schmitzer-Torbert et al., 2005) are conventions, not validated thresholds, and they depend on the features used.

**Sampling bias.** Extracellular methods favor large, active neurons. Shoham, O'Connor and Segev (2006) argued that a large fraction of cortical neurons are nearly silent. "Typical" firing properties from sorted units may therefore describe a vocal minority.

**Identity, not just isolation.** Cell typing from waveform shape is fragile. **Optotagging** combines tetrodes with optogenetics: when a genetically defined population expresses channelrhodopsin, units that fire at short, reliable latency to light pulses are tagged as that type (Lima et al., 2009). Beware spikes driven indirectly through synapses. These arrive later and with more jitter.

**Chronic tracking.** Claiming the same neuron across days from waveform similarity alone is risky, because drift and plasticity alter waveforms. Stable autocorrelograms, firing rates and functional fingerprints provide supporting evidence.

**Modern tooling.**
- SpikeInterface (Buccino et al., 2020) runs many sorters through one framework and compares their outputs.
- SpikeForest (Magland et al., 2020) benchmarks sorters on ground-truth and hybrid datasets, in which synthetic spikes are injected into real recordings. A sobering finding: sorters often agree on high-amplitude units but diverge on small ones.
- Human curation in tools like Phy remains standard, but it adds operator variability.

**Toward the clinic.** In epilepsy monitoring, Behnke-Fried depth electrodes carry eight microwires that emerge from the tip. Recordings from these, sorted with Wave_clus, revealed human "concept cells," such as the famous unit that responded to images of Jennifer Aniston (Quiroga et al., 2005). Microwire bundles lack the tight geometry of a tetrode, so isolation is weaker and multi-unit labels are common.

**Open questions** include fully automated, reproducible sorting with honest uncertainty estimates for each spike, and correcting electrode drift without human judgment.

keyPoints: A tetrode is four twisted fine wires whose tips sit tens of micrometers apart
Each neuron makes a distinct amplitude pattern across the four wires, allowing separation
Spike sorting pipeline: filter, detect, align, extract features, cluster, check quality
Refractory-period violations flag clusters that mix neurons (multi-unit activity)
Ground-truth studies (Harris et al., 2000) showed sorting errors are real and measurable
Bursting, overlaps, drift and silent neurons bias what sorted units can tell us

test.q: A tetrode is:
choices: A disc electrode on the scalp
A sixteen-site silicon shank
A bundle of four fine wires
A single glass pipette electrode
test.explain: A tetrode is four insulated wires twisted together so their tips sit close enough to record the same neurons.

test.q: Why can a tetrode separate neighboring neurons better than a single wire?
choices: Its larger tip picks up signals from more distant cells
Each cell gives a different height pattern across wires
It stimulates each cell so the cell fires on command
It penetrates the membrane to record voltage inside cells
test.explain: Spike amplitude falls with distance, so each neuron produces its own pattern of amplitudes on the four wires. A tetrode records outside cells, not inside them.

test.q: To isolate spikes, the raw tetrode signal is usually filtered to roughly which band?
test.explain: Spikes last about a millisecond, so a band of about 300 Hz to 6 kHz keeps them and removes slower field potentials.

test.q: A cluster contains many inter-spike intervals shorter than 1 ms. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: The signal was filtered at too high a cutoff
The cluster likely merges two or more neurons
The electrode has drifted away from the soma
The neuron is firing in a normal burst pattern
test.explain: One neuron cannot fire again within its refractory period of about 1-2 ms, so such intervals suggest mixed cells. Bursts have intervals of a few milliseconds, not under 1 ms.

test.q: Wilson and McNaughton's 1993 tetrode study was a landmark because it:
choices: Mapped grid cells in entorhinal cortex
Introduced the glass patch pipette
Recorded dozens of place cells at once
Discovered orientation tuning in cortex
test.explain: Using multiple tetrodes, they recorded dozens of hippocampal place cells at the same time and decoded the rat's position from the ensemble. Grid cells were found later, in 2005.

test.q: Why is spike-detection noise often estimated from the median absolute signal rather than the standard deviation?
choices: The median is faster for computers to calculate
The median removes slow drift of the electrode
Standard deviation ignores negative voltages
Spikes would inflate the standard deviation
test.explain: Large spikes push the standard deviation up and raise the threshold too high. The median-based estimate (median divided by 0.6745) resists them.

test.q: In spike sorting, principal component analysis is used to:
choices: Compress waveforms into a few features
Remove 50 or 60 Hz line noise
Lower the impedance of the electrode tips
Stimulate neurons near the electrode tips
test.explain: PCA reduces each waveform to a few numbers that capture most of its variation, which makes clustering easier.

test.q: Why are tetrode tips often gold-plated?
choices: To block slow signals such as brain waves
To make the wires stiff enough to enter tissue
To insulate the four wires from one another
To lower impedance and reduce thermal noise
test.explain: Gold plating increases the effective tip surface and lowers impedance, which reduces noise. Filtering, not plating, removes slow signals.

test.q: In hippocampal tetrode data, a unit with a very brief waveform and a high firing rate is most likely a putative:
choices: Dentate granule cell
Fast-spiking interneuron
Reactive astrocyte
Pyramidal projection neuron
test.explain: Narrow waveforms and high rates are the classic signature of fast-spiking interneurons. Pyramidal cells have broader spikes, lower rates and bursts, and astrocytes do not fire spikes.

test.q: Clusters that mix spikes from several neurons are often labeled ___ activity instead of single units.
test.explain: Multi-unit activity (MUA) still carries information, but it cannot be attributed to one neuron.

test.q: What term describes an experimenter manually drawing boundaries around groups of points in feature space to define units?
test.explain: Cluster cutting, done in programs like MClust, is the manual alternative to automated clustering such as KlustaKwik.

test.q: The two-wire precursor of the tetrode, introduced in 1983, was called the ___.
test.explain: McNaughton, O'Keefe and Barnes introduced the stereotrode, and the four-wire tetrode extended the idea.

kidTest.explain: Each cell's beep looks a bit different on each wire, so scientists can tell the cells apart.

An electric beep from a cell

kidTest.explain: Brain cells talk using tiny electric beeps called spikes.

advancedTest.q: On one tetrode, two clusters have nearly identical amplitude ratios across the four wires. One cluster sits at lower overall amplitude, and many of its spikes follow spikes of the other cluster by a few ms. The best interpretation is:
choices: Electrode drift moved the tetrode between two layers
One bursting cell whose later spikes shrink in amplitude
Two neighboring pyramidal cells fire in tight synchrony
An interneuron is driven monosynaptically by a pyramidal cell
advancedTest.explain: Identical channel ratios imply the same source location, and amplitude decrement at intervals of a few ms is typical of CA1 complex-spike bursts. A separate interneuron would sit elsewhere and give different ratios.

advancedTest.q: Cross-correlograms between pairs of units on the same tetrode show a consistent dip within about 1 ms of zero lag, but pairs on different tetrodes do not. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Each cell's refractory period spreads to adjacent cells
Gap-junction coupling delays spikes in adjacent neurons
Strong monosynaptic inhibition links nearby neuron pairs
Overlapping waveforms are missorted or lost to dead time
advancedTest.explain: Near-synchronous spikes on the same tetrode sum into hybrid waveforms or fall in detector dead time, so they are lost. That a dip appears only for same-tetrode pairs points to a methodological artifact, not biology.

advancedTest.q: Anatomy predicts about a thousand neurons within 140 µm of a CA1 tetrode, yet only about a dozen units are isolated. Which explanation is best supported?
choices: Gold plating blocks signals from neurons beyond roughly 10 µm away
Many cells fire too sparsely or weakly to form separable clusters
Insertion damage silences the majority of neurons near the tips
Sorting software tends to merge interneurons into the noise cluster

lessons.title: High-Density Probes: Neuropixels and Silicon Arrays

levels.kid:
Brain cells talk to each other with tiny electric sparks called **spikes**. Older tools could listen to only a few cells at a time. That is like pressing one ear against one door in a giant apartment building.

Scientists wanted to hear lots of cells at once. So they built a special probe called **Neuropixels**. It is a super thin needle made from the same stuff as computer chips. It is about as wide as a hair and about as long as your fingernail.

Along the needle sit almost 1,000 tiny listening spots. Little computer parts built into the probe gather all the signals. That means scientists can hear hundreds of cells at the same time, in many brain areas. It is like hearing a whole orchestra instead of one violin!
levels.hs:
**Extracellular recording** means placing an electrode outside neurons to pick up the small voltage changes made when nearby cells fire **spikes** (action potentials). Classic setups used one metal wire or a few, which could hear only a handful of neurons.

**High-density probes** solve this with the same technology used to make computer chips. Engineers carve a thin needle, called a **shank**, out of **silicon** and pattern many tiny metal **recording sites** along it. Each active site connects to a **channel**, the electronics that amplify and record its signal.

The most famous is **Neuropixels**, released in 2017 by a team that included HHMI's Janelia campus, the Allen Institute, University College London and the Belgian chip-research center **imec**. One probe:
- Has a shank about 10 mm long and 70 µm wide, roughly the width of a hair
- Carries 960 recording sites
- Records 384 channels at the same time

Because the sites sit about 20 µm apart, each neuron shows up on several neighbouring sites, which helps scientists tell neurons apart. One probe can cross several brain regions, from the cortex down to the thalamus.

Real example: in 2019, Nick Steinmetz and colleagues used Neuropixels to record about 30,000 neurons across 42 brain regions in mice doing a visual decision task. Signals related to action and engagement turned out to be spread widely across the brain, not confined to a few areas.
levels.college:
High-density probes are microfabricated silicon devices that put many recording sites on thin shanks. Two important ancestors:
- **Michigan probes** (Ken Wise, University of Michigan, from the 1970s): planar silicon shanks with sites patterned by photolithography. Commercial versions (such as NeuroNexus probes) offer multi-shank layouts with tens of sites.
- **Utah array** (Richard Normann, University of Utah, 1990s): a 10 × 10 grid of 100 silicon needles, each with one site at its tip, sampling a patch of cortex in two dimensions. It was later used in human brain-computer interfaces.

**The wiring bottleneck.** On a passive probe, every site needs its own wire running up the shank to an external amplifier. More sites mean more wires and a wider, more damaging shank. Neuropixels solved this with **CMOS** (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) circuits built into the probe. On-probe amplifiers and filters condition each signal, and **multiplexers** time-share many channels over a few output lines, with digitization on the probe base. A switch matrix selects which 384 of the 960 sites are active.

**Neuropixels 1.0 (Jun et al., Nature 2017):**
- 10 mm shank with a 70 × 20 µm cross-section
- 960 **titanium nitride** sites (12 × 12 µm), 384 simultaneous channels
- Each channel split into an **AP band** (spikes, about 0.3-10 kHz, sampled at 30 kHz) and an **LFP band** (slow field potentials from summed synaptic currents, below about 500 Hz)
- Noise around 5 µV rms, low enough to resolve small spikes

**Neuropixels 2.0 (Steinmetz et al., Science 2021):** smaller and lighter, with single-shank or four-shank versions (up to 5,120 sites), built for chronic implants in freely moving mice and for following neurons across weeks.

**Why density matters.** A neuron's extracellular spike is detectable only within roughly 50-100 µm and shrinks with distance. Closely spaced sites capture each neuron's spatial footprint, which improves spike sorting and lets software correct for **drift**, the slow movement of brain tissue relative to the probe.
levels.phd:
**Spatial sampling.** The extracellular action potential is dominated by transmembrane currents near the soma and axon initial segment, and its amplitude falls steeply with distance. The pattern of amplitudes and waveform shapes across neighbouring sites forms a near-unique signature for each neuron, and dense geometry allows source localization, estimating each unit's position along and across the shank. Neuropixels 1.0 arranges sites in a staggered four-column checkerboard at 20 µm vertical pitch, so 384 contiguous channels span 3.84 mm. Neuropixels 2.0 uses two aligned columns at 15 µm pitch (384 sites span 2.88 mm), a regular lattice that simplifies spatial interpolation.

**Drift registration.** Brain tissue moves tens of micrometres relative to the probe from respiration, pulsation and slow settling. Because sampling is dense, the depth distribution of spike amplitudes over time can be used to estimate displacement and re-register the data, as in Kilosort 2.5 onward and methods such as DREDge. Uncorrected, one neuron gets split into several clusters or merged with a neighbour.

**Landmark studies:**
- **Steinmetz et al. 2019 (Nature):** about 30,000 neurons in 42 regions during visual discrimination; choice and action signals were distributed across many areas, and engagement modulated activity brain-wide.
- **Stringer et al. 2019 (Science):** with eight simultaneous probes, much ongoing forebrain activity, including in visual cortex, tracked spontaneous facial movements. Apparent task signals therefore need to be checked against movement.
- **Siegle et al. 2021 (Nature, Allen Brain Observatory):** six probes across visual cortical areas and thalamus revealed a functional hierarchy from response timing.
- **International Brain Laboratory:** a standardized task and pipeline across labs produced a brain-wide map from hundreds of insertions.

**Nuance.** Unit yields are biased toward neurons with large, frequently firing spikes, such as big pyramidal cells and fast-spiking interneurons. Sparsely firing cells contribute too few spikes for sorting templates, so few responsive neurons in a region may reflect detectability rather than biology. Axonal spikes also inflate counts. **Neuropixels Ultra** (about 6 µm pitch) resolves footprints finely enough to aid cell-type classification and detect axonal signals. A live debate is whether brain-wide distributed coding reflects real computation or widespread movement and arousal signals.
levels.expert:
**Practical pipeline.** Insertions are typically slow, a few micrometres per second near the target, to limit dimpling and compression. Many labs coat shanks with a lipophilic dye such as DiI so the track can be reconstructed histologically and aligned to the Allen Common Coordinate Framework, then refined using electrophysiological landmarks such as LFP signatures and silent white-matter bands. The choice of reference, the probe tip or an external electrode, strongly shapes LFP interpretation. A single 384-channel probe produces tens of gigabytes per hour, so open tools such as SpikeInterface, the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) format and the DANDI archive have become standard infrastructure.

**Chronic and cross-species use.** Recoverable implants (for example Juavinett et al. 2019) let one probe be reused across animals, cutting cost. A primate version, Neuropixels 1.0 NHP, extends the shank to about 45 mm with thousands of sites to reach deep structures in macaques.

**Human recordings.** In 2022, Paulk et al. (Nature Neuroscience) and Chung et al. (Neuron) reported intraoperative Neuropixels recordings in patients undergoing procedures such as deep brain stimulation or tumor or epilepsy resection, capturing many single units in human cortex. The hard problems were brain pulsation and respiration-driven motion far larger than in head-fixed mice, short recording windows, and strict sterility and safety review.

**Biocompatibility limits.** Stiff silicon is mismatched to soft brain. **Micromotion** drives a foreign-body response, with microglial activation, an astrocytic **glial scar**, and local neuronal loss that degrade signals over months; long-implanted Utah arrays in brain-computer interface users show gradual signal decline. Flexible alternatives, including polymer probes from Loren Frank's lab, Charles Lieber's mesh electronics and Neuralink's polymer threads, flex with the tissue and aim for more stable long-term yields.

**Open questions:**
- Validation: paired juxtacellular recordings give ground truth for only a few cells, so error rates of automated sorting are hard to pin down.
- Scaling: power dissipation, tissue heating and data bandwidth constrain how many sites can be active at once.
- Integration: probes combining recording with on-shank light emitters for optogenetics are in development, promising causal tests at the same site.

Ancestors: Michigan probes (Ken Wise) and the 10 x 10 Utah array (Richard Normann)
Neuropixels 1.0: 10 mm shank, 960 titanium nitride sites, 384 channels at once
On-probe CMOS amplifiers and multiplexers beat the one-wire-per-site bottleneck
Dense sites capture each neuron's spatial footprint, aiding sorting and drift correction

lessons.title: Local Field Potentials and Neural Oscillations

levels.kid:
Your brain has billions of cells called neurons. They talk using tiny electrical signals. Scientists can listen with a very thin wire called an **electrode**.

Some electrodes listen to one cell, like hearing one friend's voice. But the slow part of the signal is more like a microphone hanging over a stadium. You can't hear one person, but you can hear the whole crowd. This crowd sound is called a **local field potential**.

When many cells work in step, the crowd sound rises and falls in **waves**, like fans chanting together. In deep sleep the waves are slow and big. When you are busy and alert, they get faster. During sleep, quick little bursts called **ripples** help your brain save the day's memories.
levels.hs:
Neurons communicate with electrical signals. Instead of poking an electrode inside a cell, scientists can place one in the fluid **outside** neurons. This **extracellular** electrode picks up two kinds of signal at once:

- **Spikes**: brief, sharp blips (about 1 millisecond long) from the action potentials of the few neurons right next to the tip.
- The **local field potential (LFP)**: a slower, wavier signal produced by the combined activity of thousands of neurons around the electrode, mostly from currents flowing at synapses.

Scientists separate the two with **filters**. The fast part (roughly 300 to 6,000 Hz) holds the spikes. The slow part (below about 300 Hz) is the LFP.

When many neurons are active in rhythm, the LFP shows **neural oscillations**, named with Greek letters:
- **Delta** (about 1-4 Hz): deep sleep
- **Theta** (about 4-10 Hz in rodents): exploring and navigating
- **Alpha** (8-12 Hz): relaxed wakefulness
- **Beta** (13-30 Hz): holding a posture steady
- **Gamma** (about 30-80 Hz): active processing and attention

A classic example: in the 1960s Cornelius Vanderwolf recorded from the rat hippocampus, a memory region. He found a strong theta rhythm whenever the rat ran or explored, and during REM (dreaming) sleep. The rhythm faded when the rat sat still. Oscillations like this help coordinate the timing of neurons across brain regions.
levels.college:
The extracellular potential is the voltage, measured against a distant reference, created as ions flow across neuronal membranes into and out of the surrounding fluid. Inward current at one spot (a **current sink**) must be balanced by outward current elsewhere on the same cell (a **source**), which forms a tiny **dipole**.

**What generates the LFP**
- **Synaptic currents** dominate. Excitatory input to the apical dendrites of a pyramidal cell creates a sink there and a source near the soma. Synaptic currents last tens of milliseconds, so they sum well across neurons.
- Other contributors include dendritic calcium spikes, afterhyperpolarizations and, at higher frequencies, action potentials themselves.
- Geometry matters. In cortex and hippocampus, pyramidal cell dendrites are aligned in parallel (an **open field**), so their dipoles add up. Where dendrites are radially symmetric (a **closed field**), the dipoles cancel and little LFP appears.

**Key rhythms and their circuits**
- **Theta** (rodent hippocampus, ~4-10 Hz): paced by the medial septum, which sends GABAergic and cholinergic input.
- **Gamma** (~30-80 Hz): a loop between pyramidal cells and fast-spiking **parvalbumin (PV) basket cells**. Rhythmic inhibition opens brief windows for firing (the **PING** model).
- **Sharp-wave ripples**: during quiet waking and slow-wave sleep, a burst from CA3 drives a 'sharp wave' in CA1 topped by a 150-250 Hz ripple. Place cells replay recent paths, and ripples are thought to support **memory consolidation**.
- **Slow oscillation** (<1 Hz): in deep sleep, cortical neurons alternate between active 'up' and silent 'down' states.

Rhythms interact. Gamma amplitude often peaks at a preferred theta phase, which is called **phase-amplitude coupling**.

**Localizing the source**
Fields spread through conductive tissue (**volume conduction**), so an LFP can reflect sources millimetres away. A **laminar probe** records across cortical layers and enables **current source density (CSD)** analysis. Taking the second spatial derivative of the LFP over depth reveals where sinks and sources actually sit.
levels.phd:
Extracellular fields obey volume-conductor theory. In the quasi-static approximation, brain tissue behaves as a largely ohmic medium (conductivity on the order of 0.3 S/m). The potential at any point is therefore the distance-weighted sum of all transmembrane currents. A single neuron's dipole field decays roughly as 1/r², but synchronous, aligned populations generate fields measurable over millimetres. Buzsáki, Anastassiou and Koch (2012) wrote the canonical review. Typical LFP amplitudes range from tens of microvolts to about a millivolt.

**CSD** follows from Poisson's equation. Assuming homogeneous, isotropic conductivity, CSD is proportional to the negative second spatial derivative of the potential (Nicholson and Freeman 1975; Mitzdorf 1985). Kajikawa and Schroeder (2011) showed that the LFP recorded in a region can be dominated by distant generators, while CSD stays local. This is a central reason to report CSD whenever laminar data exist.

Spectral analysis uses multitaper Fourier methods, wavelet transforms, or band-pass filtering followed by the **Hilbert transform** to extract instantaneous phase and amplitude. Two caveats dominate current practice:
- Power spectra combine oscillatory peaks with an **aperiodic 1/f-like component**. A broadband change in slope can masquerade as a band-power change. Parameterization tools (specparam, formerly FOOOF; Donoghue et al. 2020) separate the two.
- **High-gamma** power (above ~80 Hz) tracks local multi-unit firing, partly because spike waveforms leak into that band (Ray and Maunsell 2011).

Classic findings link rhythms to coding. O'Keefe and Recce (1993) discovered **phase precession**: a place cell fires at progressively earlier theta phases as the rat crosses its place field. Cardin et al. and Sohal et al. (2009) generated gamma by optogenetically driving PV interneurons, establishing a causal circuit mechanism. Girardeau et al. (2009) showed that electrically disrupting ripples impairs spatial learning, and Fernández-Ruiz et al. (2019) found that optogenetically prolonging ripples improves it.

Coupling measures carry biases. The **phase-locking value** is inflated when spike counts are low, so Vinck et al. (2010) introduced **pairwise phase consistency** as an unbiased alternative. Sharp, non-sinusoidal waveforms can produce spurious phase-amplitude coupling, for example in Tort's modulation index. It remains debated whether gamma actively routes information ('communication through coherence', Fries) or is a by-product of excitation-inhibition dynamics.
levels.expert:
The same physics that makes LFPs hard to localize also makes them clinically useful. They are large, stable over years, and recordable from electrodes that would struggle to hold single units.

**Closed-loop neuromodulation.** In Parkinson's disease, LFPs recorded from deep brain stimulation (DBS) leads show exaggerated **beta** (13-30 Hz) activity in the subthalamic nucleus. This beta activity falls with levodopa and with stimulation. Tinkhauser and colleagues showed that prolonged **beta bursts** track rigidity and bradykinesia better than average beta power. Sensing-enabled implants now use this signal to adjust stimulation automatically, and in 2025 the FDA approved Medtronic's BrainSense Adaptive DBS. Practical problems include stimulation artifact, beta peaks that vary between patients, and contamination from the heart's electrical signal.

**Pharmaco-electrophysiology.** Drugs leave reproducible spectral fingerprints that translate from rodent LFP to human EEG, which makes them useful target-engagement biomarkers in drug discovery. NMDA antagonists such as ketamine raise gamma power, consistent with reduced excitatory drive onto PV interneurons and disinhibition of pyramidal cells. Benzodiazepines, which are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors, raise beta power. Parameterize the aperiodic component before claiming a band-specific drug effect.

**Linking to imaging.** Logothetis and colleagues (2001) recorded neural activity during fMRI in monkeys. They found that the BOLD signal was better predicted by LFP than by spiking, implying that BOLD reflects synaptic input and local processing more than neuronal output.

**Recording pitfalls.**
- A reference electrode placed in active tissue injects its own signal, so compare bipolar, common-average and remote references.
- Chewing, whisking and movement create artifacts in the same bands as theta and gamma.
- Line noise (50/60 Hz) sits inside the gamma band.

**Open questions.**
- **Ephaptic coupling**: fields can alter neuronal excitability directly (Anastassiou et al. 2011), so the LFP may be partly causal rather than a pure readout.
- **40 Hz stimulation**: Iaccarino et al. (2016) reported that driving gamma reduced amyloid in Alzheimer's model mice. Soula et al. (2023) found that 40 Hz light neither entrained native hippocampal gamma nor lowered amyloid. The field remains divided while human trials continue.
- Can high-density laminar recordings map which cell types and pathways generate each rhythm in behaving animals?

LFPs arise mainly from summed synaptic currents in aligned neurons (open fields)
Oscillation bands: delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma, plus sharp-wave ripples
PV basket cells drive gamma; the medial septum paces hippocampal theta
Volume conduction spreads fields; laminar CSD localizes sinks and sources
LFP beta guides adaptive DBS, and drugs leave spectral fingerprints

Their dendrites line up in parallel

advancedTest.q: After a drug, spectral power rises at every frequency with no distinct peak, and the authors claim a stronger beta rhythm. What alternative should be tested first?
choices: Faster theta phase precession in CA1
Stronger synchrony among beta generators
A shift in the aperiodic 1/f component
Higher impedance at the electrode tip
advancedTest.explain: A broadband change without a peak suggests a change in the aperiodic component, which tools like specparam can separate. Stronger beta synchrony is the claim being tested, not the alternative.

advancedTest.q: Spike-field locking measured with the phase-locking value looks stronger for a neuron that fired few spikes. Why?
choices: Few spikes shift the LFP toward gamma
The PLV is biased upward with few spikes
Low spike counts reduce volume conduction
Sparse firing neurons are truly more locked
advancedTest.explain: The phase-locking value is inflated at low sample sizes. Pairwise phase consistency (Vinck et al. 2010) removes this bias.

lessons.title: Multielectrode Arrays for Cultures, Slices and Retina

levels.kid:
Imagine a tiny glass plate, smaller than a cracker, with lots of shiny metal dots in the middle. Each dot works like a super-tiny **microphone**.

Scientists grow brain cells on top of the plate. Sometimes they lay a very thin slice of brain on it, or a small piece of an eye.

Brain cells talk with quick electric clicks called **spikes**. The metal dots hear these clicks from outside the cells, without poking holes in them. Because there are many dots, scientists can hear lots of cells at once. It is like hearing a whole choir instead of one singer.

With this plate, scientists can watch young brain cells learn to click together. They can see how a piece of eye answers to light. They can also test whether a new medicine calms cells that click too much.
levels.hs:
A **multielectrode array (MEA)** is a flat chip, usually glass, with dozens to thousands of tiny metal electrodes built into its surface. Living nerve tissue sits directly on top. Each electrode picks up the small voltage changes that happen just outside nearby neurons when they fire **action potentials** (spikes).

This is **extracellular recording**: the electrodes never pierce the cells. That has two big advantages:
- You can record from **many cells at once**, which lets you study networks rather than single neurons.
- Because the cells are not damaged, you can record the **same culture for days to weeks**, watching activity change as the network grows.

MEAs can also **stimulate**: passing a small current through an electrode can make nearby neurons fire.

Three common preparations sit on MEAs:
- **Cultures**: neurons grown in a dish, including human neurons made from stem cells.
- **Brain slices**: thin living sections of brain, often the hippocampus.
- **Retina**: the light-sensing tissue from the back of the eye, which keeps working in a dish and can be stimulated with real images.

A real example: in 1994, Markus Meister, Jerome Pine and Denis Baylor placed a piece of salamander retina on a 61-electrode array. They recorded many ganglion cells (the retina's output neurons) at the same time while showing it patterns of light, revealing how groups of cells encode a visual scene together.

The signals are tiny, only millionths of a volt, so careful amplification is essential.
levels.college:
**Construction.** The first planar MEA (Thomas and colleagues, 1972) recorded beating chick heart cells; Guenter Gross and Jerome Pine adapted the approach for neurons in the late 1970s and 1980. A classic commercial chip has 60 electrodes in an 8 x 8 grid (corners omitted), each roughly 10-30 µm wide and spaced about 200 µm apart. Electrodes are made of titanium nitride, platinum or gold, connected by insulated tracks, sometimes transparent indium tin oxide so cells can be viewed under a microscope. Multiwell plates put a small array in each of dozens of wells for screening.

**Signals.** An extracellular spike on an MEA is typically **tens to hundreds of microvolts**, far smaller than the roughly 100 mV action potential measured inside a cell. Amplitude falls steeply with distance, so each electrode hears mostly the few closest neurons. Data are high-pass filtered (around 200-300 Hz) for spikes and low-pass filtered for slower field potentials. Spikes are detected when the signal crosses a **threshold**, commonly set at about 5 times the noise standard deviation.

**Cultures.** Dissociated rodent cortical or hippocampal neurons form synapses and, by roughly the second week in vitro, fire **network bursts**: brief episodes in which many neurons fire together. Firing rate, burst rate and synchrony are standard readouts.

**Slices.** Acute hippocampal slices let you evoke field EPSPs and study plasticity across many sites at once. Adding a GABA-A receptor blocker such as bicuculline or picrotoxin removes inhibition and produces **epileptiform** (seizure-like) activity. Tissue on flat glass gets poor oxygen from below, so **perforated MEAs** with holes allow perfusion from underneath.

**Retina.** The retina is placed **ganglion cell layer down** on the electrodes, and light reaches the photoreceptors from above. Flickering **white-noise** stimuli plus **spike-triggered averaging** map each ganglion cell's receptive field.

**Heart cells.** In stem-cell-derived cardiomyocytes, the **field potential duration (FPD)** serves as an in-vitro stand-in for the ECG **QT interval**.
levels.phd:
**Coupling physics.** A neuron on a planar electrode is separated from it by a thin electrolyte-filled cleft, tens of nanometres high. In Peter Fromherz's **point-contact model**, membrane current flowing through the patch facing the electrode passes through the cleft's **seal resistance**, generating the voltage the electrode reads. The recorded waveform therefore reflects transmembrane current (dominated by capacitive and Na+ currents), not the intracellular voltage, and it often looks like a scaled derivative of the action potential. Weak adhesion lowers seal resistance and signal. Noise is set by electrode impedance (thermal noise) and amplifier noise, which is why rough, high-surface-area coatings such as titanium nitride, platinum black or the conducting polymer PEDOT are used: they lower impedance without enlarging the footprint.

**High-density CMOS MEAs.** Integrating amplifiers under the electrodes allows dense grids: MaxWell's chips have 26,400 electrodes at 17.5 µm pitch, with a switch matrix routing 1,024 to readout; 3Brain's BioCam arrays have 4,096 electrodes. At this density every neuron spreads its spike over many electrodes, producing a spatial **footprint** that supports template-based spike sorting and lets you follow action potentials along unlabeled axons (Bakkum and colleagues, 2013), measuring conduction velocity in situ.

**Classic retinal work.** Meister, Wong, Baylor and Shatz (1991) used an MEA to show that the developing ferret retina generates **spontaneous retinal waves**: correlated bursts sweeping across ganglion cells before eye opening, now thought to help refine visual connections. Alan Litke and E.J. Chichilnisky later built 512-electrode arrays; Field and colleagues (2010) used one with cone-sized stimuli to map functional inputs from individual cones to identified primate ganglion cells.

**Culture dynamics.** Wagenaar, Pine and Potter (2006) tracked dissociated rat cortical cultures for weeks and found an extremely rich repertoire of bursting patterns, including superbursts. A long-running debate asks how much this bursting reflects real circuit computation versus a deafferented network lacking normal input; high-frequency distributed stimulation can suppress bursting, supporting the deprivation view.
levels.expert:
**Drug safety and screening.** MEAs are now a regulatory-grade tool. In the FDA-led CiPA (Comprehensive in vitro Proarrhythmia Assay) effort, human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes on multiwell MEAs were used to detect drugs that delay repolarization: hERG potassium-channel blockers such as E-4031 prolong field potential duration and can trigger early afterdepolarization-like events. The US EPA developed multiwell MEA network formation assays in rat cortical cultures to screen chemicals for developmental neurotoxicity.

**Disease modelling.** Patient iPSC-derived neurons on MEAs model channelopathies and neurodevelopmental disorders, for example SCN1A variants in Dravet syndrome and MECP2 in Rett syndrome, using firing and burst phenotypes as readouts that a candidate drug may normalize. Trujillo and colleagues (2019) reported that cortical organoids develop increasingly complex oscillatory network activity over months on MEAs. For neurosurgery, cortical tissue resected during epilepsy or tumour surgery can be kept as human slices on MEAs, giving rare access to living adult human circuits.

**Retinal prostheses.** Chichilnisky's group used dense arrays to stimulate primate ganglion cells electrically with single-cell, sometimes cell-type, selectivity, a blueprint for high-fidelity prosthetic vision.

**Pitfalls.**
- **Pseudoreplication**: electrodes in one well share a network and are not independent; the culture or well is the unit of analysis, ideally across several independent differentiations.
- **Maturation**: iPSC neurons and cardiomyocytes stay relatively fetal-like; when you record changes the answer.
- **Sampling bias**: electrodes favour large, active, well-adhered cells; silent neurons are invisible.
- **Analysis choices**: threshold level and burst-detection algorithm can create or erase a phenotype.
- **Environment**: temperature, CO2/pH, medium changes and evaporation shift firing; retinas bleach under strong light.

**Open questions.** How to record from the interior of 3D organoids (flexible mesh and 3D electrodes are emerging), how to combine MEAs with optogenetics and imaging for cell-type identification, and how to interpret claims of in-vitro learning: the 2022 DishBrain study, in which cultures on a high-density array improved at a Pong-like task, drew strong criticism for overstating its findings.

keyPoints: An MEA is a chip of many electrodes that records spikes from outside cells
Noninvasive recording allows many cells to be followed for days to weeks
Cultures, brain slices and retina are the main MEA preparations
Extracellular spikes are tens to hundreds of microvolts, detected by thresholds
High-density CMOS arrays reveal spike footprints and axon propagation
MEAs drive drug safety, neurotoxicity and iPSC disease-model screening

test.q: What is the full name of the device abbreviated MEA?
test.explain: MEA stands for multielectrode array: a chip with many electrodes that record from tissue placed on top.

test.q: How do the electrodes of an MEA record from neurons?
choices: By measuring light from a calcium-sensitive dye
From outside the cells, without piercing them
Through a glass pipette sealed onto the membrane
Through a wire pushed into the cell body
test.explain: MEAs record extracellularly, picking up voltage changes just outside cells. A sealed glass pipette describes patch clamp, not MEAs.

test.q: What is a major advantage of MEAs compared with patch clamp?
choices: Recording many cells for days to weeks
Seeing single ion channels open one at a time
Controlling the voltage across one membrane
Measuring exact subthreshold voltages inside a cell
test.explain: Because MEAs do not damage cells, they can follow many neurons in the same culture over long periods. Intracellular voltage and voltage control are strengths of patch clamp.

test.q: How is a piece of retina usually positioned on an MEA?
choices: Ganglion cell layer facing the electrodes
Lens and cornea still attached on top
Photoreceptor layer facing the electrodes
Optic nerve threaded through a central hole
test.explain: The retina's output neurons, the ganglion cells, are placed on the electrodes, while light reaches the photoreceptors from above.

test.q: In MEA studies of cultured cortical neurons, what is a 'network burst'?
choices: Slow calcium waves spreading through glial cells
One neuron firing a single unusually large spike
Brief episodes of many neurons firing together
Bursts of electrical noise from damaged electrodes
test.explain: Network bursts are synchronized episodes of firing across many neurons, typically emerging around the second week in vitro.

test.q: About how large is an extracellular spike recorded by an MEA electrode?
choices: Tens to hundreds of microvolts
Tens to hundreds of millivolts
A few nanovolts per spike
One to two volts per spike
test.explain: Extracellular spikes are in the microvolt range, far smaller than the roughly 100 mV action potential measured inside a cell.

test.q: With stem-cell-derived heart muscle cells on an MEA, field potential duration is a stand-in for which ECG measure?
choices: The resting heart rate
The QT interval
The P wave width
The PR interval
test.explain: Field potential duration reflects the time from depolarization to repolarization, like the QT interval, so drugs that prolong it raise arrhythmia concerns.

test.q: Adding a GABA-A receptor blocker to a hippocampal slice on an MEA is used to produce:
choices: Long-term depression of synapses
Seizure-like epileptiform activity
Growth of new axon branches
Silencing of action potential firing
test.explain: Blocking GABA-A receptors removes fast inhibition, so excitation runs unchecked and epileptiform bursts appear.

test.q: Which method maps the receptive fields of retinal ganglion cells on an MEA?
choices: Darkness followed by one brief flash of light
Electrical pulses delivered to the optic nerve
White-noise flicker with spike-triggered averaging
Bright steady light while counting total spikes
test.explain: Averaging the random stimulus that preceded each spike reveals the pattern of light a cell responds to, its receptive field.

test.q: Perforated MEAs were developed for brain slices mainly to:
choices: Hold dissociated neurons firmly in place
Lower the cost of making each chip
Let light reach the photoreceptor layer
Improve oxygen and fluid flow to tissue
test.explain: A slice on flat glass gets poor oxygen from below; holes allow perfusion from underneath so the tissue stays healthy.

test.q: Spikes are detected when the signal crosses a ___ set at several times the noise level.
test.explain: A threshold, often about 5 times the noise standard deviation, separates spikes from background noise.

test.q: Which eye tissue did Meister, Pine and Baylor record on a 61-electrode array in 1994?
test.explain: They recorded many retinal ganglion cells at once from salamander retina while presenting light patterns.

kidTest.q: What are the metal dots on the plate like?
choices: Tiny magnets
Tiny microphones
Tiny flashlights
kidTest.explain: Each dot listens to the cells, like a little microphone.

kidTest.q: How do brain cells talk to each other?
choices: Quick electric clicks
Small sounds you can hear
Drops of colored liquid
kidTest.explain: Brain cells send quick electric signals called spikes.

kidTest.q: Why is it useful to have lots of dots on the plate?
choices: To make the plate stronger
To keep the cells warm and cozy
To hear many cells at once
kidTest.explain: More dots means scientists can listen to a whole choir of cells, not just one.

kidTest.q: What do scientists lay on the plate to see how it answers to light?
choices: A piece of ear
A piece of eye
A piece of skin
kidTest.explain: A piece of eye still responds to light, so scientists can watch its cells click.

kidTest.q: The quick electric clicks brain cells make are called s _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Spikes are the quick electric signals brain cells use to talk.

advancedTest.q: On a high-density CMOS MEA, one neuron's spike appears large on a few electrodes and small on many others. The best use of this footprint is to:
choices: Confirm that the neuron is inhibitory, not excitatory
Sort spikes into units using their spatial templates
Measure single-channel currents beneath the soma
Estimate the neuron's resting membrane potential precisely
advancedTest.explain: The spatial pattern of amplitudes across electrodes is a signature for each neuron, enabling template-based spike sorting. Extracellular signals do not report resting potential or single-channel currents.

advancedTest.q: A study claims a drug lowers firing, treating 2,000 electrodes from 3 cultures as independent samples. What is the main flaw?
choices: Three cultures give an excessively large sample
Having many electrodes lowers statistical power
Electrodes in one culture are not independent
Firing rate is not measurable with planar MEAs
advancedTest.explain: Electrodes share one network, so this is pseudoreplication; the culture or well is the true unit, ideally across independent differentiations.

advancedTest.q: Field and colleagues (2010) mapped inputs from individual cones to identified primate ganglion cells. This required combining:
choices: Cone calcium imaging and optic nerve shocks
Whole-cell patch clamp and full-field flashes
Single tungsten wires and drifting gratings
Dense arrays and cone-sized light stimuli
advancedTest.explain: A 512-electrode array recorded many ganglion cells at once, while stimuli fine enough to hit single cones revealed each cone's input. Full-field flashes cannot resolve individual cones.

advancedTest.q: A compound prolongs field potential duration in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes on an MEA. The most likely interpretation is that it:
choices: Slows the upstroke, as sodium blockers do
Silences beating, as cell death would do
Shortens the plateau, as calcium blockers do
Delays repolarization, as hERG blockers do
advancedTest.explain: Field potential duration tracks repolarization like the QT interval; hERG potassium-channel blockers such as E-4031 prolong it, the signal CiPA-style assays look for.
